previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with low-grade fever, malaise, and increased abdominal distension. He had recently been exposed to a family member with cold symptoms. Workup included negative blood, urine, and ascites cultures, ruling out bacteremia and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Imaging showed stable cirrhosis and new but non-urgent findings in the liver and lung. His symptoms were attributed to a viral upper respiratory infection, which improved with supportive care including fluticasone. A therapeutic paracentesis removed 2 liters of fluid. Nutrition recommended reducing tube feeding duration from 18 to 16 hours daily due to suspected caloric excess. He remained stable on his transplant regimen, including Remodulin for portopulmonary hypertension. He was discharged home with improved symptoms and follow-up planned with his liver team.
problems: Acute upper respiratory infections of unspecified site
Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, without mention of bleeding
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ was admitted to the surgical service with known 
cirrhosis for which he had been on the transplant list for a 
year.  On ___, he underwent a deceased donor liver 
transplant which was uncomplicated. The reader is referred to 
the operative note for further details.  In the immediate 
post-operative period, he was stable and not requiring any 
pressors.  He was maintained on his home dose of remodulin for 
pulmonary hypertension as well as a nitric oxide gtt in order to 
maintain mean pulmonary artery pressures less than 40mmHg.    He 
subsequent underwent a liver duplex that show patent vasculature 
however with slightly elevated velocities in the main hepatic 
artery.  Liver function test were trended and demonstrated 
decreasing transaminases and bilirubin levels.  On POD1,  he was 
weaned off of the nitric oxide gtt and started on TID sildenafil 
for his pulmonary hypertension, again maintaining low PA 
pressures.  He did desat shortly after however but had a 
negative bronch and shortly recovered on his own.  Tacrolimus 
was started in addition to his already administered 
immunosuppressants including MMF and methylprednisone.  On POD2, 
he was extubated without problem.  He maintained his O2 sats and 
had low PA pressures.  Given his stable PA pressures the 
Swan-ganz catheter was removed.  Drain outputs were noted to be 
high (with serosangiouness) output and as such he was given 
fluid replacement with alubmin (12.5g per 2L of drain output).  
He was subsequently advanced to the liver pathway protocol.  On 
POD4 he was transferred to the floor in stable condition.  
Immunosuppression was continued and changed according to trough 
level measured each morning.  Prophylactic antibiotics were 
administered according to protocol.  The valcyte was reduced in 
the setting of acute renal failure.  Over the next 3 days, he 
was again maintained on the liver transplant pathway. He 
remained hemodynamically stable, afebrile, had downtrending 
LFT's, resolving renal failure, and worked with ___ to regain his 
strength.  Also in the setting and in conjunction with the 
Pulmonary team his remodulin was turned down from 44 to 42ng/kg 
which he seemed to tolerated well. 

On POD8, Mr. ___ was found to be acutely tachycardic and 
tachypneic.  Given the findings, he was transferred to the 
surgical intensive care unit where a full set of labs and a 
liver duplex were obtained.  His transaminases were noted to be 
dramatiacally elevated.  His liver duplex showed a patent but 
stenotic hepatic artery.  There was a slight area of hepatic 
infarct however this was felt not to be contributing to his 
symptoms.  Over the next few hours he continued to decompensate 
and was eventually intubated.  Shortly there after, increasing 
amounts of pressors were required.  The decision was made to 
image using a CT scan which demonstrated gas-formng abscess in 
the liver.  Exploratory laparotomy was performed but no driage 
of the abscess could be performed; necrotic liver was debrided.  
See the OP note for furter details. Into POD9, he increasingly 
had a pressor requirement and maxed out on 4 agents.  He went 
into renal failure and reqired CVVH.  In conjunction with his 
health care proxy the decision was made to no longer pursue 
aggressive measures.  He expired shortly after.  Cultures from 
the exploration revealed E.coli in the liver and his blood cx 
were consistent with an E. coli bacteremia.  

We suspect the liver had been seeded with E Coli prior to 
donation as the donor had a history of IV drug use.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  End-stage renal disease, liver transplant.  Pre-op evaluation.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior chest radiographs including most recent from ___ and scout image from abdominal/pelvic CT from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  PA and lateral chest radiographs.  

FINDINGS:

An enteric tube courses below the diaphragm, tip is not included on this
examination.  A right central line terminates in the mid to lower SVC.  The
cardiac silhouette is top-normal in size, not significantly changed since
prior examination.  New right lung base opacity likely relates to atelectasis.
There is atelectasis at the left lung base.  No focal consolidation, large
pleural effusion or pneumothorax is identified.  

IMPRESSION:

New opacity in the right lower lobe is likely atelectasis.  No evidence of
pneumonia.

HISTORY:  ___ man status post liver transplant.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior radiographs the chest dated ___
through ___.

FINDINGS:

Portable semi-upright radiograph of the chest demonstrates atelectasis and
congestion at the bilateral bases.  The heart is top normal in size. 
Endotracheal tube is seen with the tip terminating 5 cm above the carina. 
Swan-Ganz catheter is seen with the tip in the right pulmonary artery.  Right
IJ seen with tip terminating in the cavoatrial junction.  A second right
internal jugular catheter is seen with the tip at the level of the thoracic
inlet.  Nasogastric tube is seen with the tip in the stomach.

HISTORY:  Status post liver transplant, evaluate patency of hepatic artery and
portal vein.

TECHNIQUE:  Liver ultrasound and Doppler.

COMPARISON:  None.

FINDINGS:

Liver Doppler:  The main portal, right portal and left portal vein are patent
with normal hepatopetal flow.  Elevated velocities are seen within the main
portal vein, reaching up to 134 cm/second, which is not unexpected within 24
hours after transplant.  The right, middle and left hepatic veins are patent. 
The main hepatic artery is patent and shows a brisk systolic upstroke.  Given
the increase in end-diastolic velocities, the resistive indices of the right
and left hepatic arteries are 0.42 and 0.38, respectively.  The IVC is patent.

Liver ultrasound:  There is no intrahepatic fluid collection.  There is a
trace amount of perihepatic ascites.  The echotexture of the liver appears
normal.  Scattered hyperechoic foci are indeterminate in etiology and may be
related to surgery, attention on follow up would be recommended.  There is no
intra or extrahepatic biliary ductal dilation.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Patent portal venous system.  Elevated portal velocities are likely
postoperative.  
2.  Normal hepatic artery acceleration with increased diastolic flow yielding
decreased resistive indices.  While this is likely due to the early
postoperative state, followup ultrasound ___ hr after transplant would
be useful to exclude stenosis.

HISTORY:  Liver transplantation.

FINDINGS:  In comparison with the study of ___, the monitoring and support
devices are essentially unchanged.  The opacification at both bases,
especially on the right, is decreasing.

HISTORY:  ___ man status post liver transplant, status post
bronchoscopy.  Evaluate for pneumothorax.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior radiographs of the chest dated ___ to
___.

FINDINGS:

Portable semi-upright radiograph of the chest demonstrates stable bibasilar
atelectasis.  Cardiomediastinal and hilar contours are unchanged.  There is no
pneumothorax or pleural effusion.  Swan-Ganz catheter ends in the region of
the pulmonary valve.  A right-sided supraclavicular subclavian line is seen
with the tip terminating in the distal SVC.  A right internal jugular central
venous line terminates at the origin of the right brachiocephalic vein. 
Nasogastric tube is seen with tip outside the borders of this image. 
Endotracheal tube is seen at the level of the thoracic inlet, but is more than
7 cm above the carina.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No pneumothorax.

2.  ___ Ganz catheter ends in the region of the pulmonary valve; correlate
with tracing for specific localization of position.

3.  Endotracheal tube is seen with the tip at the thoracic inlet, but is more
than 7 cm from the carina.  Advance 3-4 cm for a more secured seating.

COMMENTS:  Finding #3 was discussed with Dr. ___ the SICU team by Dr.
___ at 3:30 p.m. via telephone on ___, 45 minutes after the
findings were discovered.

HISTORY:  Status post liver transplant.  

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior chest radiographs, most recently of ___.

FINDINGS:

Frontal view of the chest.  Endotracheal tube terminates 6.6 cm above the
carina.  NG tube terminates in the stomach.  Feeding tube passes into the
stomach and beyond the borders of the film.  Swan-Ganz catheter terminates in
the region of the pulmonary artery valve.  Right central venous catheter
terminates in the lower SVC.  Large-bore right IJ central catheter terminates
in the the region of right brachiocephalic vein.  

Bibasilar atelectasis is similar to prior.  No new consolidation, pleural
effusion, or pneumothorax.  Heart size and mediastinal contours are stable. 
Calcified hilar lymphadenopathy is unchanged.  

IMPRESSION:

1.  Bibasilar atelectasis without new consolidation.
2.  Swan-Ganz catheter terminates in the region of the pulmonary valve. 
Please correlate with catheter tracings.

HISTORY:  Pulmonary hypertension after liver therapy.

FINDINGS:  In comparison with the study of earlier in this date, there is some
increasing bibasilar opacification.  This could well represent more prominent
atelectatic changes, though in the appropriate clinical setting, superimposed
pneumonia would have to be considered.

The Swan-Ganz catheter tip appears to be positioned at the orifice of the
right mainstem bronchus.

Multiple densely calcified left hilar lymph nodes are again seen.

HISTORY:  Increased oxygen requirement.

FINDINGS:  In comparison with the study of ___, there are again bilateral
basilar opacifications, which appear more plate like on the left.  No definite
pneumonia, though this would be difficult to exclude in the appropriate
clinical setting.  

Allowing for differences in obliquity, there is probably little change in the
appearance of the monitoring and support devices.  Dense calcification of the
left hilar lymph nodes is again seen.

HISTORY:  Central line placement.

FINDINGS:  In comparison with study of ___, there are two central lines in
place on the right, one extending to just below the level of the carina and
the other into the right atrium.  There are lower lung volumes with extensive
areas of opacification at both bases.  Although these could represent merely
atelectatic changes, the possibility of superimposed pneumonia would have to
be seriously considered in the appropriate clinical setting.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Status post liver transplant, hypertension.

CHEST, AP:

The position of the tip of the left subclavian line has been withdrawn and now
lies at the cavoatrial junction.  The position of the right IJ line is
unchanged.

The lungs are now better expanded than they were on the prior chest x-ray,
though some areas of atelectasis are still present.  No failure is present.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH:

INDICATION:  Cirrhosis, evaluation for pulmonary edema.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  As compared to the previous radiograph, no relevant change is seen.
The nasogastric tube has been removed.  Lung volumes remain low, with mild
fluid overload and borderline size of the cardiac silhouette.  No pleural
effusions.  No pneumonia, minimal atelectasis at the left and right lung base
persist.

HISTORY:  Status post liver transplant now with elevated LFTs.

TECHNIQUE:  Grayscale, color, and spectral Doppler imaging of the abdomen was
performed.

COMPARISON:  Ultrasound from ___.

FINDINGS:

The liver is normal in echogenicity.  Multiple bright reflectors with dirty
shadowing are noted primarily within the left lobe but also seen within the
right lobe as well suggesting air.  There is an area of heterogeneous
echogenicity peripherally within the left lobe raising concern for infarct. 
There is no significant intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation.  The CBD could
not be visualized.  The gallbladder is absent.  The pancreas could not be
visualized due to overlying bowel gas.  The limited images of the right kidney
are grossly unremarkable.

Doppler evaluation demonstrates a patent main, right, and left portal veins
and hepatic arteries.  The elevated diastolic flow within the hepatic arteries
seen on the previous exam has decreased in the interim with the arterial
waveforms still demonstrating normal systolic peaks and acceleration times. 
Markedly elevated velocities (150-200+cm/sec) are again noted in the main
portal vein similar to the prior exam with a significant decrease in velocity
noted within the right and left intrahepatic portal veins.  These findings
raise concern for a portal venous stenosis.

IMPRESSION:

1. New foci of gas within the liver involving both lobes, but much more
notable in the left lobe.  There is also a focal peripheral area of decreased
echogenicity within the left lobe raising concern for infarct.

2. Persistently elevated main portal vein velocities similar to the previous
exam with notably discrepant lower velocities within the intrahepatic right
and left portal veins.  Findings raise concern for a portal venous stenosis. 
Further evaluation with CTA is recommended given this finding as well as the
gas seen in the liver noted above.

These findings were communicated to Dr. ___ at 9:00 on ___.

HISTORY:  ___ male with pulmonary hypertension, status post liver
transplant and acute respiratory failure.  Evaluate for endotracheal tube

FINDINGS:

Portable semi-upright radiograph of the chest demonstrates persistently low

IMPRESSION:  
1.  Endotracheal tube ends 7 cm above the carina, at the level of the superior

2.  ___-Ganz catheter ends in the distal right pulmonary artery, and should

HISTORY:  New orogastric tube.  

COMPARISON:  Same day chest radiograph at 10:47 AM.  

FINDINGS:

Single frontal view of the chest.  Orogastric tube passes into the stomach
with its tip beyond the limits of the film.  Endotracheal tube is in unchanged
position with its tip at the level of the superior margin of the clavicles. 
Swan-Ganz catheter terminates in the distal right pulmonary artery, similar to
prior.  Right IJ central venous catheter terminates at the cavoatrial
junction.  Right subclavian catheter terminates in the mid SVC.  Lung volumes
remain low with bibasilar atelectasis.  No pneumothorax.  Heart size and
cardiomediastinal contours are stable.  

IMPRESSION:

1.  OG tube passes into the stomach with its tip beyond the limits of the
film.  

2.  ET tube and Swan-Ganz catheter are in unchanged position.  Advancement of
the ET tube by 2-3 cm and withdrawal of the Swan-Ganz catheter by 3-4 cm is
again recommended.

HISTORY:  Status post liver transplant, tachycardia and hypoxia. Assess for
pulmonary embolus as well as questionable wedge infarction on recent
ultrasound.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial images were acquired through the chest during the
pulmonary arterial phase of enhancement with 130 mL of Omnipaque. 
Subsequently, a CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed during the venous
phase of enhancement.  Coronal and sagittal reformations were provided and
reviewed.

DLP:  972 mGy/cm.

COMPARISON:  Liver ultrasound degenerative tear ___.

FINDINGS:

CTA chest:  The timing of contrast limits evaluation for subsegmental
pulmonary emboli.  Within this limitation, there are no large filling defects
to indicate a pulmonary embolus.  An apparent filling defect within the right
upper lobe pulmonary artery is thought to relate to flow artifact or a lymph
node (6:  108).  The aorta and main pulmonary artery are normal in caliber. 
Diffuse enlargement of the peripheral pulmonary arteries may indicate
underlying portal pulmonary syndrome.  

An endotracheal tube is in satisfactory position.  Debris is seen surrounding
the inflated cuff.  The airways are patent through the segmental level. 
Collapse or consolidation are seen within the lower lobes bilaterally.  There
is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  A small focus of ground-glass opacity
is seen in the left upper lung (6:76).  

The heart is mildly enlarged.  A Swan Ganz catheter is present, terminating
within the right main pulmonary artery.  A right-sided tunneled hemodialysis
catheter terminates in the right atrium.  There is no supraclavicular,
axillary or or central lymphadenopathy.  

Abdomen:  The patient is status post a liver transplant.  There are 2 large
infarctions involving almost the entirety of the left lobe, the largest
measuring 11.5 x 8.9 cm.  Both collections show internal loculated air and
branching air consistent with pneumobilia.  Hypodensities are also seen
peripherally in the right lobe worrisome for infarction as well.  Fluid fills
the hila and extends into the region of the duodenum.  Periportal
lymphadenopathy is unchanged from prior.  A intermediate common hyperdense 3.5
x 3.3 cm collection displaces the native inferior vena cava laterally and may
indicate an underlying hematoma (8: 17).  An abdominal drain is positioned
posterior to the liver.  

The timing of contrast limits complete evaluation of the hepatic vasculature. 
The portal venous system appears patent however, there is an abrupt transition
in caliber between the extra and intrahepatic main portal vein.  This, in
part, is thought secondary to significant periportal edema.  The known
replaced main hepatic artery is not optimally visualized but presumed patent
given the findings on the same day liver ultrasound.  The superior mesenteric
artery is patent.  The left hepatic vein is diminutive.  Markedly enlarged
splenic varices are present and unchanged.  

The spleen remains markedly enlarged.  Scattered calcifications are consistent
with prior granulomatous disease.  There is a small amount of ascites
scattered throughout the abdomen and pelvis.  The pancreas and adrenal glands
are unremarkable.  

A wedge shaped hypodensity is seen in the posterior right kidney consistent
with infarction (8: 26).  There is no hydronephrosis.  A simple cyst seen in
the upper pole of the right kidney is unchanged.  

The stomach is unremarkable.  An enteric tube terminates within the body of
the stomach.  There is diffuse thickening of small bowel which may relate to
portal congestion.  There is no evidence for obstruction.  The large bowel is
unremarkable.  

Pelvis:  A Foley catheter is present.  The rectum is unremarkable.  There is
no inguinal or pelvic sidewall lymphadenopathy. 

Bones and soft tissues:  Fusion hardware is seen at L5-S1.  Multilevel
compression deformities, worst at T9, are unchanged.  There is anasarca.  

IMPRESSION: 1.  Timing of contrast severely limits the evaluation for
pulmonary embolus, however, there is no large pulmonary embolus seen.  2. 
Infarctions involve almost the entirety of the left lobe and are scattered
peripherally in the right lobe.  Timing of the contrast limits evaluation of
the hepatic vasculature, however, the replaced main hepatic artery is likely
patent given the findings on the same day ultrasound.  3.  Abrupt change in
caliber from the intra to extrahepatic main portal vein.  While this may
indicate stenosis, there is likely an element of mass-effect from significant
periportal edema.  4.  Peripheral infarction in the right kidney.  5.  Diffuse
small bowel thickening may relate to portal congestion.  6.  Bilateral lower
lobe consolidations.  7.  Dilated pulmonary vasculature consistent with portal
pulmonary syndrome.  

These findings were discussed with Dr. ___ by Dr. ___ at 17:18 on ___ 5 min after discovery.
